title: The Double Diamond
author: The Good Boss
source: The Good Boss on Substack, December 8, 2025
summary: The opening anecdote does most of the work. At a design thinking workshop, the author heard a story about NASA exploring ways to keep astronauts fit on long missions. Someone floated sending a Peloton bike into orbit, and the idea gathered momentum on the grounds that astronauts need exercise and if Musk can send a Tesla, NASA can send a Peloton. Then one team member asked a different question: what is the problem we are trying to solve? That reframe, from 'send a bike into orbit' to 'keep astronauts healthy in zero gravity,' collapsed the Peloton. The eventual solution was a resistance band. Cheap, light, effective. Note for the archive: the free portion of this newsletter ends at the start of Stage 1 (Discover), so the detailed stage-by-stage walkthrough sits behind the paywall. The framework and the anecdote that anchor the argument are delivered in full in the open text. The author generalises the trap. Leaders chase clever fixes because solutions are fun to talk about and problems are not. They jump to solution space before they have diagnosed the problem space, and the cost of solving the wrong problem is higher than they think. The Double Diamond, developed by the British Design Council, is the proposed corrective. Its job is to force a separation most teams blur: the problem space where you slow down, explore, and figure out what is actually wrong, and the solution space where you start thinking about how to fix it. The shape is two diamonds end-to-end because both halves have the same rhythm: diverge (open up), then converge (narrow down). The four stages are named in the free portion: Discover (explore the problem from all angles), Define (identify the real problem worth solving), Develop (explore possible solutions), and Deliver (test and launch the best one). The archived use, even without the full walkthrough, is the discipline itself. Before authorising the resources for a solution, ask the NASA question. What outcome are we actually chasing, and is the thing we are about to build the simplest way to produce it. For a primary leader or EdTech decision-maker, this is the filter that stops a new platform from being procured to solve a problem that turns out to be a timetabling, onboarding, or communication issue in disguise.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: NASA was once exploring ways to keep astronauts fit during long space missions. Someone on the NASA team floated an idea that became an instant hit: Send a Peloton bike into space. It sounded wild at first, but not totally unreasonable.

But then, just as this idea was gaining traction, someone on the team asked a different question: What’s the problem we’re trying to solve? Or, put another way, “Are we trying to send a bike into orbit? Or are we trying to keep astronauts healthy in zero gravity?

That simple shift in perspective changed how NASA approached this. Eventually, instead of a heavy, expensive, over-engineered bike, the solution turned out to be, wait for it, a resistance band. Cheap, light and effective.
Fundamentally, what the astronauts really needed wasn’t a bike. They needed fitness, and that needed tension, which could be delivered through a simple resistance band.

As leaders, that’s the trap that most of us fall into at work. We chase “clever” fixes, and sometimes fail to identify the “real” problem. We jump at solutions before we identify the problem we’re trying to solve.

Sometimes, the hardest part of leadership isn’t solving the problem, it’s knowing what the problem actually is. The Double Diamond gives you a way to zoom out before you zoom in. It helps you to look at the full picture, not just the part that’s loudest or most visible.

At its core, it helps you separate two things most teams blur together: The problem space: where you slow down, explore, and figure out what’s really going wrong. The solution space: where you start thinking about how to fix it.

The Double Diamond works in four stages: Discover: explore the problem from all angles. Define: identify the real problem worth solving. Develop: explore possible solutions. Deliver: test and launch the best one.” Archived from The Good Boss on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
